transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what's been bringing you in, or what's been on your mind lately?

Well, I guess since I stopped working, I just… I can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving all day, going from one little job to the next around the house, like there’s still a crew waiting on me or something. I’ll start fixing one thing, then notice another, and then I’m outside messing with something else. It’s funny, when I was working that made sense, you know? There was always something to do. But now it’s like my body didn’t get the message that I’m retired.
Over this same period, have you noticed that you need less sleep than usual but still feel full of energy the next day?

I don’t know that I’d say that, no. I mean, I’ve never been the world’s best sleeper, but needing less sleep and then feeling great the next day… I’m not sure. Some mornings I’m up early, but then I’m just up, you know? My neighbor gets up at dawn to walk his dog, and I’ll see him out there and think I should be doing something too—but I don’t think it’s like I’m running on no sleep and feeling wonderful.
Aside from feeling like you need to stay busy, have you also been worrying excessively about a number of different things—like your health, finances, or family—more days than not?

I’m not sure I’d call it excessive worrying. I mean, everybody worries some, right? Bills come in, you hear about somebody getting sick, my brother-in-law had this whole thing with his roof last year and it got me thinking I should check my gutters… but that’s more just stuff that pops up. I don’t think I’m sitting around worrying about all of it all day, more days than not.
Did this feeling of needing to stay constantly busy start right around the time you retired, or were you feeling this kind of restlessness or unease even before you stopped working?

I think it really became a problem after I retired from the handyman work—about, what, a year and two months ago now. Before that I was always busy anyway, going from one job to another, and that was just the rhythm of it. You know, somebody’s cabinet door, then a leaky faucet, then you’re running to the hardware store because the screw you thought would fit doesn’t fit—there was always a reason to be moving. But after I stopped, that’s when it started standing out more, like I didn’t know what to do with myself if I wasn’t fixing something.
Aside from keeping busy, have you noticed feeling on edge, irritable, tense, or unable to relax on most days—even during moments when you're not doing any tasks?

I don’t know… I mean, I can get a little annoyed if I’m sitting too long, but I wouldn’t say I’m on edge all the time. Tense, maybe if there’s something I feel like I ought to be doing—like if I notice the screen door sticking, then I start thinking about where I put the screwdriver, and then that reminds me I still haven’t organized the garage. But if you mean just sitting there for no reason feeling wound up most days, I’m not sure I’ve noticed that exactly.
Has this constant need to stay busy or restlessness been causing real distress for you, or getting in the way of things like relationships, hobbies, or enjoying your retirement?

Yeah… I guess it has, more than I like to admit. My wife’s had to kind of take over keeping the calendar, because I’ll say I’m going to be somewhere or help with something and then I lose track of it. She checks behind me now, which I don’t love, but she’s usually right.

And I’ve had to apologize more than once to the folks at the community center, and the garden group too, because I said I’d do something and then… well, I let people down. I don’t mean to. I’ll get going on one thing, then notice something else that needs doing—like the shed latch or the hose reel—and next thing you know I’ve missed what I was supposed to show up for. So yeah, it’s gotten in the way some.

Before you retired, even outside of work, did you ever have this same tendency to lose track of tasks or get easily distracted moving from one thing to another, or is this pattern something new that's only shown up since you stopped working?

Oh no, that’s not brand new. I mean, it’s worse now that I don’t have a workday holding me in place, but I’ve always had that thing where my attention just… jumps tracks.

Like if I’m trying to paint something, or even plan out a little story in my head, and then I hear a truck go by outside, or I suddenly think, “Oh, I should check the garden,” that’s it—I’m over there now. And then I come back and I’ve lost the spot I was in. It’s frustrating, because I’ll have a good idea and then it’s just gone. So yeah, that part’s been around before retirement too.
Thinking back to when you were a kid, say before age 12—did you have similar trouble staying focused, like drifting off task, daydreaming, or jumping from one thing to another at school or at home?

Yeah, I think so. Back in grade school, teachers used to say I was bright, but… scattered, that was the word I heard a lot. I’d lose pencils all the time—though everybody lost pencils, I suppose, but I was always borrowing one.

And I’d call out answers before I was supposed to, then get told to raise my hand. Or I’d start my work and then somehow be staring out the window or fiddling with something, and the teacher would have to remind me, “Finish that before recess.” Funny, I can still picture the old classroom pencil sharpener on the wall… but yes, that sort of thing was there even then.
Back then, did those attention and impulsivity issues cause problems for you both at school and at home, or was it mainly noticeable in just one of those settings?

I’m not completely sure, honestly. School I remember better, because teachers wrote things down and my mother would hear about it. At home… I know I got fussed at some, but it’s harder to separate from just normal kid stuff.

I mean, we had chores and all that, and my dad was particular about things being done a certain way—he had this whole routine with the garage, every tool had a spot, and if you put the wrench back wrong he’d know immediately. Sorry, I’m wandering.

I’d say it was definitely noticed at school. At home, probably some too, but I don’t have as clear a memory of whether it caused real problems there.
In day-to-day conversations or activities now, do you often find yourself interrupting others, blurting things out, or having trouble waiting your turn?

Yes, I do that sometimes. Not constantly, but enough that I notice it—especially in the storytelling group I go to. Someone will be halfway through making a point, and I’ll already have the answer or a thought in my head, and I just jump in before they’re finished.

Then the second it’s out of my mouth I realize, oh, I cut them off. I feel bad about it, because I don’t mean to be rude. It’s more like the thought pops up and I’m afraid I’ll lose it if I don’t say it right then.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports lifelong pattern of inattention, distractibility, impulsivity, and restlessness beginning before age 12 (documented at school), persisting into adulthood, and causing functional impairment across multiple settings (missed commitments, relational friction with spouse, community group obligations). Symptoms are chronic and trait-like rather than episodic, ruling out a manic/hypomanic episode (no decreased need for sleep with increased energy, no euphoria/grandiosity) and are not better explained by generalized anxiety (patient explicitly denies pervasive excessive worry or anxious tension unrelated to tasks).
